questions.q: What circumstances was Paul trying to avoid by not coming to the Corinthian church?
questions.a: Paul was avoiding coming to the Corinthian church in sorrow.

questions.q: Why did Paul write as he did in his previous epistle to the Corinthian church?
questions.a: He wrote as he did so that when he came to them he might not be hurt by those who should have made him rejoice.

questions.q: When Paul wrote to the Corinthians before, what was his state of mind?
questions.a: He was in great tribulation and anguish of heart.

questions.q: Why did Paul write this letter to the Corinthian church?
questions.a: He wrote to them so that they would know the depth of the love that he had for them.

questions.q: What did Paul say the Corinthian saints should now do for the one they punished?
questions.a: Paul said they should forgive and comfort that person.

questions.q: Why did Paul say the Corinthian saints should forgive and comfort the one they had punished?
questions.a: This was so that the one they had punished would not be overwhelmed by too much sorrow.

questions.q: What is another reason Paul wrote to the Corinthian church?
questions.a: Paul wrote to them to test them and to find out whether they were obedient in everything.

questions.q: Why was it important for the Corinthian church to know that whoever they had forgiven was also forgiven by Paul and in the presence of Christ?
questions.a: This was so that Satan would not trick them.

questions.q: Why did Paul have no peace of mind when he went to the city of Troas?
questions.a: He had no peace of mind because he could not find his brother Titus in Troas.

questions.q: What did God do through Paul and his companions?
questions.a: Through Paul and his companions God spread the sweet aroma of the knowledge of Christ everywhere.

questions.q: How did Paul say that he and his companions were different from many people who sold the word of God for profit?
questions.a: Paul and his companions were different in that they spoke with purity of motives, as sent from God, speaking in Christ in the presence of God.

commentary.text: Reasons for the apostle not coming to Corinth.
Directions about restoring the repentant offender.
An account of his labours and success in spreading the gospel of Christ.

Verses 1–4 The apostle desired to have a cheerful meeting with them; and he had written in confidence of their doing what was to their benefit and his comfort; and that therefore they would be glad to remove every cause of disquiet from him. We should always give pain unwillingly, even when duty requires that it must be given.

The apostle desires them to receive the person who had done wrong, again into their communion; for he was aware of his fault, and much afflicted under his punishment. Even sorrow for sin should not unfit for other duties, and drive to despair. Not only was there danger last Satan should get advantage, by tempting the penitent to hard thoughts of God and religion, and so drive him to despair; but against the churches and the ministers of Christ, by bringing an evil report upon Christians as unforgiving; thus making divisions, and hindering the success of the ministry. In this, as in other things, wisdom is to be used, that the ministry may not be blamed for indulging sin on the one hand, or for too great severity towards sinners on the other hand. Satan has many plans to deceive, and knows how to make a bad use of our mistakes.

A believer's triumphs are all in Christ. To him be the praise and glory of all, while the success of the gospel is a good reason for a Christian's joy and rejoicing. In ancient triumphs, abundance of perfumes and sweet odours were used; so the name and salvation of Jesus, as ointment poured out, was a sweet savour diffused in every place. Unto some, the gospel is a savour of death unto death. They reject it to their ruin. Unto others, the gospel is a savour of life unto life: as it quickened them at first when they were dead in trespasses and sins, so it makes them more lively, and will end in eternal life. Observe the awful impressions this matter made upon the apostle, and should also make upon us. The work is great, and of ourselves we have no strength at all; all our sufficiency is of God. But what we do in religion, unless it is done in sincerity, as in the sight of God, is not of God, does not come from him, and will not reach to him. May we carefully watch ourselves in this matter; and seek the testimony of our consciences, under the teaching of the Holy Spirit, that as of sincerity, so speak we in Christ and of Christ.
